meta.title: Paper 2 Traps
meta.note: Paper 2 is 90 marks, the largest pool in the exam, and almost none of it is lost through not knowing enough. It is lost through the same twenty or so mistakes, made under time pressure, in a paper where most sections give no part credit. This module names every one of them, gives the fix, and gives a rescue routine for the moment you meet a word you do not know.
howToUse: Read one section before you drill that section, not after. A trap you have read about that morning is a trap you notice.
The Rescue tab is the one to know by heart. It is what you do when knowledge runs out and there are still four minutes left.
Filter by cost. Anything marked Costs marks every time is worth more attention than a rare trap.
The word lists in Rescue are the words PSLE uses in campaign posters and non-narrative passages. They are not story words, which is exactly why they catch people out.

paperShape.bookletA: 25 marks, MCQ, auto-marked. No part credit at all: a near-miss scores the same as a blank.
paperShape.bookletB: 65 marks, open response. Part credit exists on Synthesis (1 grammar + 1 meaning) and on most Open-Ended items.
paperShape.pacingRule: About 30 minutes on Booklet A and 80 on Booklet B. If you are behind at the halfway point, abandon the cloze blanks you are stuck on and come back to them; the Open-Ended is worth 20 marks and cannot be rushed.

sections.label: Grammar MCQ
sections.oneLine: Ten items on tense, subject-verb agreement, articles, prepositions and pronouns. Decide by rule, never by ear.
routine: Find the real subject of the verb and cross out everything between it and the verb.
Ask what the tense has to be, using the time words in the sentence as evidence.
Read each option into the full sentence, not just into the gap.
Eliminate on a rule you can name. If you cannot name the rule, you are guessing by sound.

traps.trap: Agreeing the verb with the nearest noun instead of the real subject
traps.wrong: The box of chocolates were on the table.
traps.right: The box of chocolates was on the table.
traps.why: The words between the subject and the verb are there on purpose. Your ear hears chocolates and matches to it.
traps.fix: Cross out everything between the subject and the verb with your pencil, then read what is left: the box was.

traps.trap: Treating each, every, either, neither and one of as plural
traps.wrong: Each of the boys have a locker.
traps.right: Each of the boys has a locker.
traps.why: Of the boys sits next to the verb and sounds plural, but the subject is each, which is always singular.
traps.fix: These five are singular no matter what follows: each, every, either, neither, one of.

traps.trap: Mixing up a number of and the number of
traps.wrong: The number of students have increased.
traps.right: The number of students has increased. / A number of students have complained.
traps.why: The two phrases look almost identical but take opposite verbs.
traps.fix: THE number = one figure = singular. A number = several = plural.

traps.trap: Not using the past perfect for the earlier of two past events
traps.wrong: By the time the bell rang, the students finished their lunch.
traps.right: By the time the bell rang, the students had finished their lunch.
traps.why: Both events are in the past, so simple past feels right for both.
traps.fix: If one past thing happened before another past thing, the earlier one takes had. Look for by the time, before, after, already, when.

traps.trap: Using the present perfect with a finished time word
traps.wrong: She has visited her grandmother yesterday.
traps.right: She visited her grandmother yesterday.
traps.why: Have and has feel more formal, so they get chosen for formal-sounding sentences.
traps.fix: Yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago and just now all forbid have and has. Present perfect needs an unfinished time: since, for, already, yet, ever, never, so far.

traps.trap: Since and for the wrong way round
traps.wrong: He has lived here since five years.
traps.right: He has lived here for five years. / He has lived here since 2021.
traps.why: Both appear with the present perfect, so they blur together.
traps.fix: SINCE takes a point in time (since Monday, since he was six). FOR takes a length of time (for two hours, for five years).

traps.trap: Guessing the preposition after a verb
traps.wrong: The result depends of the weather.
traps.right: The result depends on the weather.
traps.why: Prepositions after verbs are fixed by habit, not by logic, so there is nothing to reason from.
traps.fix: Learn them as whole phrases: depend on, consist of, apologise for, congratulate on, insist on, accuse of, blame for, prefer to, succeed in, participate in, comment on, differ from, capable of, similar to, responsible for.

traps.trap: Choosing a or an by the letter instead of the sound
traps.wrong: an university / a hour
traps.right: a university / an hour
traps.why: The rule is taught as before a vowel, which is a rule about spelling rather than speech.
traps.fix: The rule is about the SOUND the next word starts with. University starts with a you sound, so a. Hour starts with an ow sound, so an. Also: an honest boy, a European, an X-ray, a one-way street.

traps.trap: Wrong pronoun case in a pair
traps.wrong: The prize was shared between my brother and I.
traps.right: The prize was shared between my brother and me.
traps.why: And I has been corrected into people so often that it starts to sound right everywhere.
traps.fix: Delete the other person and read it again: between me sounds right; between I does not.

traps.trap: An adverb where the sentence needs an adjective
traps.wrong: The soup tastes badly.
traps.right: The soup tastes bad.
traps.why: The -ly form feels more correct because it is used for describing how things are done.
traps.fix: After be, seem, look, feel, taste, smell, sound and become, use an adjective. These verbs describe the thing, not the action.

traps.trap: Neither and nor agreeing with the wrong half
traps.wrong: Neither the teacher nor the students was ready.
traps.right: Neither the teacher nor the students were ready.
traps.why: The first noun is usually the one your ear latches onto.
traps.fix: With either/or and neither/nor, the verb matches the subject NEARER to it.

traps.trap: A question tag that does not match the sentence
traps.wrong: She has finished her homework, hasn't it?
traps.right: She has finished her homework, hasn't she?
traps.why: The tag gets built from the wrong word, usually the nearest noun.
traps.fix: The tag copies the auxiliary and the subject, and flips the polarity. Positive sentence gets a negative tag, and the other way round. Remember the odd one: I am late, aren't I?

traps.trap: Reflexive pronouns used as ordinary subjects
traps.wrong: My friend and myself went to the library.
traps.right: My friend and I went to the library.
traps.why: Myself sounds more polite and more formal.
traps.fix: Use myself only when you are also the one doing it: I hurt myself. Otherwise use I or me.

traps.trap: Agreeing with a collective noun as though it were plural
traps.wrong: The team are travelling to Malaysia.
traps.right: The team is travelling to Malaysia.
traps.why: British usage allows both and pupils hear both, but PSLE marking treats a collective noun acting as one unit as singular.
traps.fix: Team, class, family, government, committee and crowd act as one body: use the singular verb.

sections.label: Vocabulary MCQ
sections.oneLine: Five items. The right answer is the one the sentence demands, not the one you have heard of.
routine: Cover the options and predict the missing word yourself first.
Decide what part of speech the gap needs.
Decide whether the missing word is positive or negative from the words around it.
Plug each surviving option back into the whole sentence and read it in your head.

traps.trap: Choosing the word you recognise
traps.wrong: Picking the familiar option because the others look strange.
traps.right: Picking the option the sentence needs, even if you have never seen it before.
traps.why: An unfamiliar word feels risky, so the brain avoids it. Examiners know this and use a familiar near-miss as the main distractor.
traps.fix: Test every option against the sentence, including the ones you do not know. An unknown word is not evidence of a wrong word.

traps.trap: Ignoring the part of speech the gap needs
traps.wrong: Putting a noun where the sentence needs an adjective.
traps.right: Checking the slot first: does a describing word, a doing word or a naming word belong here?
traps.why: Options are often the same root in different forms: succeed, success, successful, successfully.
traps.fix: Look at what sits immediately before and after the gap. After a or the, a naming word is coming. After was or were, a describing word usually is.

traps.trap: Missing the signal that flips the meaning
traps.wrong: Reading only the half of the sentence with the gap in it.
traps.right: Reading the whole sentence, including the half after the comma.
traps.why: However, although, despite, unfortunately, instead and yet all reverse the direction of the sentence, and they are often in the half people skip.
traps.fix: Circle the joining word before you choose. If it is a contrast word, the answer is the opposite of what the first half suggests.

traps.trap: Right meaning, wrong strength
traps.wrong: The loss of his pencil case left him devastated.
traps.right: The loss of his pencil case left him annoyed.
traps.why: Several options can be near-synonyms, and only one matches the size of the event.
traps.fix: Ask how big the event is, then pick the rung that matches. Options often form a ladder on purpose.

traps.trap: A word that means the right thing but does not go with its neighbours
traps.wrong: We had strong rain last night. / She did a mistake.
traps.right: We had heavy rain last night. / She made a mistake.
traps.why: The meaning is right and the grammar is right, so nothing feels wrong.
traps.fix: English fixes certain pairs by habit. Read the gap together with the word next to it and ask whether you have ever heard that pair.

traps.trap: Falling for the look-alike
traps.wrong: The film was adopted from a novel.
traps.right: The film was adapted from a novel.
traps.why: Distractors are chosen to look or sound almost the same: adapt and adopt, effect and affect, principal and principle, complement and compliment.
traps.fix: When two options differ by one or two letters, that pair is the whole question. Decide which is which before looking at the rest.

traps.trap: Leaving it blank
traps.wrong: No answer marked because none looked certain.
traps.right: The best surviving option marked, always.
traps.why: Certainty never arrives, and the clock moves on.
traps.fix: There is no penalty for a wrong MCQ answer. A blank and a wrong answer score the same, so a blank is a wasted one-in-four chance.

traps.trap: Choosing before reading to the end of the sentence
traps.wrong: Marking an answer that works for the first eight words.
traps.right: Marking an answer that works for all of them.
traps.why: The disqualifying detail is usually placed at the end.
traps.fix: Read to the full stop before you mark anything. The end of the sentence is where examiners hide the deciding word.

sections.label: Vocabulary Cloze MCQ
sections.oneLine: Five blanks in one short passage. Collocation and register decide most of them.
routine: Read the whole passage once, ignoring the blanks, so you know the topic and the tone.
Do the blanks you are sure about first; each one you fill narrows the ones you are not.
For each blank, check the word immediately after it as well as before it.
Reread the finished passage from the top. A wrong answer usually sounds wrong on the second pass.

traps.trap: Treating each blank as a separate question
traps.wrong: Filling blank 1, then blank 2, without ever reading the passage as a whole.
traps.right: Reading the passage once first, then filling.
traps.why: A vocabulary cloze is one continuous text, and the topic decides which sense of a word is meant.
traps.fix: Thirty seconds of reading first will save you two wrong answers.

traps.trap: Breaking a fixed phrase
traps.wrong: take part of the competition
traps.right: take part in the competition
traps.why: Only one of the options completes the set phrase, and the others are ordinary words that mean roughly the same.
traps.fix: Look for whole phrases rather than single words: take part in, pay attention to, make an effort, keep in touch, come to a decision, put up with, look forward to.

traps.trap: A word that is too casual for the passage
traps.wrong: The minister said the plan was a big deal for the country.
traps.right: The minister said the plan was significant for the country.
traps.why: The word means the right thing, so nothing feels wrong until you notice the passage is a news report.
traps.fix: Decide in the first read whether the passage is a story, a report or an advertisement, and pick words at that level.

traps.trap: Ignoring the preposition that follows the blank
traps.wrong: He was accused for stealing.
traps.right: He was accused of stealing.
traps.why: The preposition after the blank is fixed and it eliminates every option but one, but only if you look at it.
traps.fix: Read three words past the blank before choosing. The preposition is often the whole answer.

traps.trap: Choosing a word that contradicts the passage's position
traps.wrong: A word that praises, in a paragraph that is warning about something.
traps.right: A word that matches the writer's stance.
traps.why: Grammatically nothing is wrong, so the error is invisible at sentence level.
traps.fix: After the first read, decide in one word whether the writer is for or against. Every blank must agree with that.

traps.trap: Repeating a word the passage has just used
traps.wrong: Choosing important when important appears in the previous line.
traps.right: Choosing the option that varies the wording, if it fits.
traps.why: The familiar word feels safe because you have just read it.
traps.fix: Continuous texts avoid repeating the same word twice in two lines. If an option repeats one, it is usually the distractor.

sections.label: Visual Text Comprehension
sections.oneLine: Five items on one poster, usually a Singapore campaign. The answer is on the page, including the small print.
routine: Read every word on the visual before reading any question: headline, sub-heading, captions, small print, logos, footer.
Name the audience and the purpose in your head in one sentence each.
For every option, ask where on the poster it is supported.
Reject anything that is true in real life but not printed on the visual.

traps.trap: Reading the headline and skipping the small print
traps.wrong: Answering from the big words only.
traps.right: Answering from the whole visual, including the line at the bottom in small type.
traps.why: The small print is small precisely so that it is skipped, and at least one question is usually set on it.
traps.fix: Read the smallest text on the poster first. It takes fifteen seconds and it is where the deciding detail lives.

traps.trap: The almost-right option
traps.wrong: An option that changes one number, date, age or name.
traps.right: The option whose every detail matches the visual exactly.
traps.why: The distractor is built from the visual's own words with one thing altered, so it reads as familiar and correct.
traps.fix: Check the numbers digit by digit against the poster. Dates, ages, prices and deadlines are the usual altered details.

traps.trap: Answering with what is true, not what is stated
traps.wrong: Choosing an option because you know it is true about recycling.
traps.right: Choosing the option the poster actually says.
traps.why: General knowledge feels like evidence, and campaign topics are ones pupils already know about.
traps.fix: Point to the words on the poster that support your choice. If you cannot point, it is not the answer.

traps.trap: Confusing the topic with the purpose
traps.wrong: The purpose is to talk about dengue.
traps.right: The purpose is to persuade residents to remove stagnant water at home.
traps.why: The topic is what it is about; the purpose is what it wants you to do or feel.
traps.fix: Purpose answers always contain a verb aimed at the reader: to persuade, to warn, to inform, to encourage, to remind.

traps.trap: Getting the audience wrong
traps.wrong: Saying the audience is everyone.
traps.right: Naming the group the poster's words and pictures are aimed at.
traps.why: Everyone is never the answer, but it feels safe.
traps.fix: Look at who is pictured, what they are doing, and which words are used. Residents, students, cyclists, elderly, parents, hawkers.

traps.trap: Answering a tone question from the picture
traps.wrong: Deciding the tone is happy because the drawing is colourful.
traps.right: Deciding the tone from the words chosen.
traps.why: The image is louder than the text and is processed first.
traps.fix: Tone lives in word choice. Look for commands, exclamation marks, warnings, or gentle encouragement, and name the tone from those.

traps.trap: Missing the call to action
traps.wrong: Overlooking the line that tells the reader what to do next.
traps.right: Finding it, because a question is usually set on it.
traps.why: It is often at the very bottom, next to a website, hotline or QR code.
traps.fix: Every campaign poster has a call to action. Find it before you start the questions.

sections.label: Grammar Cloze
sections.oneLine: Ten blanks, no word bank, one word each. Most answers are small function words, not impressive ones.
routine: Read the whole passage first without writing anything.
For each blank, name the word class needed before you choose a word.
Fill the ones you are sure of, then reread from the top for the rest.
At the end, check every blank holds exactly one word and is spelled correctly.

traps.trap: Writing two words in one blank
traps.wrong: has gone / very cold
traps.right: gone / freezing
traps.why: The two-word version is often what the sentence means, so it feels like the honest answer.
traps.fix: One blank is one word, always. If two words are needed, you have misread which word is missing.

traps.trap: Reaching for an impressive word when a small one is needed
traps.wrong: Filling blanks with content words when the passage needs of, to, which, had, been, than, whose.
traps.right: Recognising that a grammar cloze mostly tests function words.
traps.why: Practice on vocabulary makes pupils look for vocabulary.
traps.fix: Before choosing, ask which class is missing. In a grammar cloze it is usually a preposition, article, auxiliary verb, relative pronoun, conjunction or quantifier.

traps.trap: Losing the tense across the passage
traps.wrong: A passage written in the past that drifts into the present halfway down.
traps.right: One tense held from the first line to the last, unless the passage deliberately changes.
traps.why: Each blank is answered on its own, so the thread is dropped.
traps.fix: Write the passage's main tense at the top of the page and check every verb blank against it.

traps.trap: The right word spelled wrongly
traps.wrong: recieve, thier, definately
traps.right: receive, their, definitely
traps.why: The thinking work is finished, so the writing is done on autopilot.
traps.fix: A misspelled answer scores zero even when the thinking was right. Reread your own handwriting at the end.

traps.trap: Leaving a blank empty
traps.wrong: A gap left because nothing came to mind.
traps.right: The most sensible word that fits the grammar, written in.
traps.why: It feels more honest to leave it than to guess wrongly.
traps.fix: An empty blank is a guaranteed zero. A grammatically sensible guess is sometimes right and never worse.

traps.trap: Ignoring the sentence that comes after
traps.wrong: Choosing a connective from the first half of the sentence only.
traps.right: Reading on to see whether the passage agrees or disagrees with itself.
traps.why: Connectives are decided by what follows, not by what precedes.
traps.fix: For any blank where a joining word might belong, read the next full sentence before choosing.

traps.trap: Messy corrections
traps.wrong: A word written over another word until neither is readable.
traps.right: One clean line through the old word and the new one written beside it.
traps.why: Corrections are made in a hurry near the end.
traps.fix: If a marker cannot read it, it is wrong. Cross out once, write clearly.

sections.label: Editing
sections.oneLine: Ten numbered lines, one error in each, roughly half spelling and half grammar. Change one word only.
routine: Read the whole passage once for meaning before changing anything.
Go line by line and ask first: is this line's error spelling or grammar?
Change exactly one word, and write the whole corrected word, not just the changed letter.
At the end, count that you have made ten changes and no more.

traps.trap: Changing a word that was already correct
traps.wrong: Correcting a line that had no error, or fixing the wrong word in a line that did.
traps.right: Leaving a word alone unless you can say what rule it breaks.
traps.why: Under pressure anything unusual starts to look wrong.
traps.fix: Name the rule before you change. If you cannot name it, move on and come back.

traps.trap: Finding two errors in one line and changing both
traps.wrong: Two corrections written on line 4.
traps.right: The single error identified and corrected.
traps.why: A line can contain a word you dislike as well as the word that is actually wrong.
traps.fix: There is one error per numbered line. If you have found two, one of them is not an error.

traps.trap: Fixing the grammar but misspelling the fix
traps.wrong: were changed to was, written as wass.
traps.right: The correction written out fully and correctly.
traps.why: Attention is on the rule, not on the letters.
traps.fix: Write the corrected word in full and reread it. A correct correction spelled wrongly earns nothing.

traps.trap: Rewriting the line instead of changing one word
traps.wrong: Reordering the sentence to make it read better.
traps.right: One word replaced, everything else untouched.
traps.why: The pupil can see a better sentence and writes it.
traps.fix: The task is a one-word substitution. A better sentence that was not asked for scores zero.

traps.trap: Correcting the grammar but changing the meaning
traps.wrong: Changing could not to can, which fixes the tense and reverses the sense.
traps.right: A correction that leaves the meaning exactly as it was.
traps.why: Only the grammar is being checked, so the meaning is not rechecked.
traps.fix: Read the corrected line back and ask whether it still says the same thing.

traps.trap: Hunting only for spelling
traps.wrong: Ten spelling changes found, and the five grammar errors missed.
traps.right: Both types looked for on every line.
traps.why: Spelling errors are visible and grammar errors are not, so the eye finds one kind and stops.
traps.fix: On each line, check spelling first, then check the verb, then check the plural. Three quick passes per line.

traps.trap: Missing an error that is a real word
traps.wrong: their where there belongs, or its where it's belongs.
traps.right: The confusable spotted, because the meaning was checked and not just the spelling.
traps.why: It is spelled correctly as a word, so a spelling check will never flag it.
traps.fix: Watch for the confusable pairs specifically: their/there/they're, its/it's, your/you're, to/too, than/then, whose/who's, weather/whether, quite/quiet, lose/loose, affect/effect.

traps.trap: Missing capital letters and proper nouns
traps.wrong: on monday, the class visited singapore zoo.
traps.right: On Monday, the class visited Singapore Zoo.
traps.why: Editing is read as a hunt for hard grammar, so the easy errors slip past.
traps.fix: Days, months, countries, names, languages and the first word of a sentence all take capitals.

traps.trap: Illegible or ambiguous corrections
traps.wrong: A correction squeezed above the line so it could be read two ways.
traps.right: The word written clearly in the space provided.
traps.why: Corrections are made at speed near the end of the section.
traps.fix: Write in the answer space, not over the line. If the marker cannot tell what you wrote, it is wrong.

sections.label: Comprehension Cloze
sections.oneLine: Fifteen blanks, no word bank, in one continuous passage. The clue is often a sentence away.
routine: Read the whole passage from start to finish without writing anything. This is not optional here.
Fill the blanks you are certain about first, wherever they are in the passage.
For the hard ones, read the sentence before and the sentence after the blank.
Reread the completed passage. Anything that sounds odd on the second read is usually wrong.

traps.trap: Filling the blanks in order
traps.wrong: Getting stuck on blank 2 and losing four minutes.
traps.right: Doing the easy ones first, so that the passage fills in around the hard ones.
traps.why: Reading left to right is a habit, and a blank feels like something that must be answered now.
traps.fix: Skip anything that does not come within ten seconds. Every blank you fill makes the remaining ones easier.

traps.trap: Looking for the clue only in the same sentence
traps.wrong: Choosing a word that fits the sentence but not the paragraph.
traps.right: Choosing a word that fits the paragraph, which is where the clue usually is.
traps.why: In a vocabulary cloze the clue is usually local, so the habit transfers.
traps.fix: In a comprehension cloze the clue is often in the previous or the following sentence. Read outward from the blank.

traps.trap: Repeating an idea the passage has already stated
traps.wrong: The rain was heavy. The heavy downpour ______ the road, making it wet.
traps.right: A word that adds the missing step: flooded.
traps.why: Repeating what has been said feels safe because it is definitely true.
traps.fix: A blank exists because something is missing. If your word only repeats the last sentence, it is not the missing thing.

traps.trap: The right idea in the wrong word form
traps.wrong: Their success depended on their ______ to work together. (write: able)
traps.right: Their success depended on their ability to work together.
traps.why: The meaning is found first and the form is not rechecked.
traps.fix: After choosing the meaning, look at what comes before the blank. After their, a naming word is needed, not a describing word.

traps.trap: Ignoring the connective logic
traps.wrong: Filling a blank after however with a word that agrees with the previous sentence.
traps.right: Filling it with something that contrasts, because however demands a turn.
traps.why: Connectives are read as decoration rather than as instructions.
traps.fix: Treat however, nevertheless, therefore, consequently, moreover and instead as arrows. They tell you which direction the next idea goes.

traps.trap: The fancy word that nearly means it
traps.wrong: Choosing a big word because it sounds like a Paper 2 answer.
traps.right: Choosing the ordinary word that exactly fits.
traps.why: The exam feels like it should reward difficult vocabulary.
traps.fix: In cloze, precision beats impressiveness every time. The ordinary right word is worth a mark; the impressive near-miss is worth nothing.

traps.trap: Leaving blanks and running out of time
traps.wrong: Three blanks unfilled because the Open-Ended was called first.
traps.right: Every blank carrying a sensible attempt before you move on.
traps.why: Fifteen blanks feels like fifteen small tasks rather than one timed block.
traps.fix: Give the cloze fifteen minutes and no more. In the last minute, fill every remaining blank with your best guess.

traps.trap: Not checking singular and plural against the passage
traps.wrong: A singular noun in a blank where the passage has been talking about several.
traps.right: A plural that matches what the passage is describing.
traps.why: The blank is answered from the sentence, and the sentence does not always show the number.
traps.fix: Ask how many the passage is talking about before you write the noun.

sections.label: Synthesis and Transformation
sections.oneLine: Five items worth two marks each: one mark for grammar, one for meaning. The meaning mark is the one most often lost.
routine: Read both original sentences and say the whole meaning to yourself in one sentence.
Look at the given word or the given opening. It tells you exactly which pattern is being tested.
Write the new sentence, keeping every piece of information and adding none.
Read your sentence against the original and check three things: same facts, same order of cause and effect, one sentence only.

traps.trap: Adding information that was not there
traps.wrong: Adding because he was tired when the original never said why.
traps.right: Only what the two original sentences contain.
traps.why: The new sentence sounds incomplete, so the gap gets filled from imagination.
traps.fix: You lose the meaning mark for anything added, even if it is a sensible guess.

traps.trap: Dropping information that was there
traps.wrong: Leaving out heavily from raining heavily, or leaving out a name.
traps.right: Every detail from both sentences carried across.
traps.why: Adverbs and small details are dropped while concentrating on the structure.
traps.fix: Underline every content word in the original. Tick each one off in your new sentence.

traps.trap: Using both joining words
traps.wrong: Although it rained, but the match continued.
traps.right: Although it rained, the match continued.
traps.why: In spoken English both halves get a signal, and it sounds balanced.
traps.fix: Pick one. Although OR but, never both. Same for because and so.

traps.trap: Despite or In spite of followed by a clause
traps.wrong: Despite it was raining, the match continued.
traps.right: Despite the rain, the match continued. / Despite it being wet, the match continued.
traps.why: Despite and although mean the same thing, so they are used the same way.
traps.fix: Despite and In spite of take a naming word or an -ing word. Although takes a full clause with its own subject and verb. Add the fact that after despite if you want a clause: despite the fact that it was raining.

traps.trap: Not continuing from the given opening
traps.wrong: Writing a fresh sentence that ignores the words already printed.
traps.right: A sentence that reads correctly when the printed opening is included.
traps.why: The printed words are read as a hint rather than as part of the answer.
traps.fix: Copy the printed opening onto your answer line and continue from it. Read the whole thing back including the printed part.

traps.trap: Writing two sentences
traps.wrong: Two full stops in an answer that was meant to combine.
traps.right: One sentence.
traps.why: Two ideas feel like they need two sentences.
traps.fix: Synthesis means joining. If you have two full stops, you have not done the task.

traps.trap: Reversing cause and effect
traps.wrong: The match continued although it rained, when the original meant the reverse relationship.
traps.right: The same direction as the original.
traps.why: Once the sentence is rearranged, which idea was the reason becomes easy to lose.
traps.fix: Before writing, say aloud which is the reason and which is the result. Then check your sentence keeps that order of ideas.

traps.trap: Grammar right, meaning changed
traps.wrong: A perfectly formed sentence that says something slightly different.
traps.right: A sentence that is both correct and identical in meaning.
traps.why: Attention goes to the structure being tested, and the meaning is assumed to have survived.
traps.fix: The two marks are separate. Check the grammar, then read the original again and check the meaning as a second, deliberate step.

traps.trap: Forgetting the back-shift in reported speech
traps.wrong: He said that he will help me.
traps.right: He said that he would help me.
traps.why: The original words are still in your head in their original tense.
traps.fix: Do the three steps in a fixed order every time: back-shift the tense, change the pronouns, change the time and place words.

traps.trap: Losing the tense in the passive
traps.wrong: The window is broken by the boy, when the original was past.
traps.right: The window was broken by the boy.
traps.why: Building the passive takes attention, and the tense is rebuilt from scratch.
traps.fix: The form of be carries the original tense. Decide the tense first, then add the past participle.

sections.label: Comprehension Open-Ended
sections.oneLine: Two passages, narrative and non-narrative. Twenty marks, and the section most often rushed.
routine: Read the questions before the passage so you know what you are looking for.
Read the passage and mark the paragraph each question points to.
Name the question type: literal, inferential, vocabulary in context, language use, purpose or personal response.
Answer with the question's own words, then the answer, then the evidence, then the explanation. Match the number of points to the number of marks.

traps.trap: Lifting a sentence straight from the passage
traps.wrong: Copying the passage's line word for word as the whole answer.
traps.right: Rewriting it in your own words, keeping the meaning.
traps.why: The passage's wording is right there and is obviously correct.
traps.fix: A direct lift shows no understanding and usually scores zero, especially when the question says in your own words. Change the verbs and the nouns, keep the meaning.

traps.trap: Ignoring the mark allocation
traps.wrong: One reason given for a question worth two marks.
traps.right: Two distinct points for two marks.
traps.why: The first point feels like a complete answer.
traps.fix: Marks equal points. Count them off before moving on. Two marks means two separate ideas, not one idea said twice.

traps.trap: Answering a different question word
traps.wrong: Explaining how, when the question asked why.
traps.right: Answering the exact question word asked.
traps.why: The passage detail is found first and the answer is built around it.
traps.fix: Circle the question word. Why needs a reason. How needs a method. What needs a thing. Suggest needs your own idea grounded in the passage.

traps.trap: Evidence with no explanation
traps.wrong: A quotation offered as the whole answer.
traps.right: The quotation followed by what it shows.
traps.why: The quotation seems to speak for itself.
traps.fix: After any quotation, write the sentence beginning This shows that. That sentence is usually where the mark is.

traps.trap: Vocabulary in context answered as a dictionary definition
traps.wrong: Giving the general meaning of the word.
traps.right: Giving what the word means in this sentence, in this passage.
traps.why: The general meaning is the one that comes to mind.
traps.fix: Read the sentence the word sits in, and write a replacement that would fit in that exact sentence.

traps.trap: Unclear pronouns in the answer
traps.wrong: He was upset because he took it.
traps.right: Rahman was upset because Wei Ming took his football.
traps.why: It is clear to the writer, who has just read the passage.
traps.fix: Name people and things in your answer. Assume the marker does not know which he you mean.

traps.trap: Personal response with nothing from the passage
traps.wrong: An opinion that could have been written without reading the text.
traps.right: An opinion anchored to something the passage actually says.
traps.why: The question invites your own view, so the passage is set aside.
traps.fix: Even a personal response needs one link back: because the passage says. Give the view, then the anchor.

traps.trap: Running out of time
traps.wrong: The last two questions answered in one line each.
traps.right: Thirty-five minutes protected for this section.
traps.why: Earlier sections feel urgent because each blank is small, so they absorb time that was budgeted here.
traps.fix: This is 20 marks, more than any other section. Check the clock at the start of Booklet B and protect this block.

traps.trap: Missing an instruction inside the question
traps.wrong: Giving two reasons where the question says give one.
traps.right: Following the instruction exactly.
traps.why: The instruction sits in brackets or in italics and reads as decoration.
traps.fix: Underline every instruction: in your own words, give two, from paragraph 3, support your answer.

traps.trap: Answering from the wrong paragraph
traps.wrong: Finding a similar-looking detail elsewhere in the passage.
traps.right: Answering from the paragraph the question names.
traps.why: Passages repeat ideas, so a plausible answer can be found in the wrong place.
traps.fix: If the question names a paragraph, put a finger on it and do not read outside it.

synthesisPatterns.note: The pattern is never hidden. The word you are given, or the opening you are given, names it. Identify the pattern first and the sentence writes itself. These are the shapes that recur across PSLE papers.

list.name: Reported speech
list.cue: said that, told me that, asked whether
list.rule: Back-shift the tense one step into the past, change the pronouns, then change time and place words. Do those three in that order.
list.wrong: "I will call you tomorrow," he said. → He said that he will call me tomorrow.
list.right: He said that he would call me the following day.
list.trap: The time word is the step people forget: tomorrow becomes the next day, today becomes that day, here becomes there, now becomes then, this becomes that.

list.name: Reported questions
list.cue: asked whether, asked if, wanted to know
list.rule: Turn the question back into statement order, drop the question mark, and use whether or if for yes-no questions.
list.wrong: She asked me where was I going.
list.right: She asked me where I was going.
list.trap: The subject and verb go back to normal order. There is no question mark on a reported question.

list.name: Although and Despite
list.cue: Although, Though, Even though, Despite, In spite of
list.rule: Although takes a full clause. Despite and In spite of take a naming word or an -ing word.
list.wrong: Despite he was tired, he finished the race.
list.right: Despite his tiredness, he finished the race. / Despite being tired, he finished the race. / Although he was tired, he finished the race.
list.trap: Never write but in the second half. One contrast word per sentence.

list.name: Relative clause
list.rule: Who for people, which for things, whose for belonging. If the clause is needed to say which one you mean, no commas. If it is extra information, put commas round it.
list.wrong: The boy which won the race is my cousin.
list.right: The boy who won the race is my cousin.
list.trap: Do not leave the old subject in as well: not the boy who he won, just the boy who won.

list.name: Active to passive
list.rule: The object moves to the front, the verb becomes a form of be plus the past participle, and the original doer follows by if it matters.
list.wrong: The window is broken by the boy yesterday.
list.right: The window was broken by the boy yesterday.
list.trap: The form of be carries the tense. Choose the tense first, then add the participle.

list.name: If-conditionals
list.rule: Type 1 real future: if plus present, will plus verb. Type 2 unreal present: if plus past, would plus verb. Type 3 changed past: if plus had plus participle, would have plus participle.
list.wrong: If he would have studied, he would have passed.
list.right: If he had studied, he would have passed.
list.trap: Would never appears in the if half. Name the type before you write.

list.name: Unless
list.rule: Unless means if not, so the verb after it stays positive.
list.wrong: Unless you don't hurry, you will miss the bus.
list.right: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
list.trap: Writing not after unless makes a double negative and reverses the meaning.

list.name: So ... that
list.rule: So goes before a describing word or an adverb: so heavy that, so quickly that.
list.wrong: It was so a heavy bag that he could not lift it.
list.right: The bag was so heavy that he could not lift it.
list.trap: So cannot take a naming word directly. If a noun follows, you need such instead.

list.name: Such ... that
list.rule: Such goes before a naming word phrase: such a heavy bag that, such loud music that.
list.wrong: It was such heavy that he could not lift it.
list.right: It was such a heavy bag that he could not lift it.
list.trap: Remember the a with a singular countable noun: such a heavy bag, but such heavy bags.

list.name: Too ... to
list.rule: Too plus adjective plus to plus verb, and the sentence must mean the thing did NOT happen.
list.wrong: The bag was too heavy so he could not lift it up.
list.right: The bag was too heavy for him to lift.
list.trap: Do not add it at the end: not too heavy for him to lift it. The object is already accounted for.

list.name: Enough to
list.rule: Enough follows an adjective and precedes a noun: strong enough to lift it, enough money to buy it.
list.wrong: He was enough strong to lift the bag.
list.right: He was strong enough to lift the bag.
list.trap: After an adjective, enough comes second. Before a noun, it comes first.

list.name: Not only ... but also
list.rule: Both halves must be the same kind of thing: two verbs, or two nouns, or two clauses. If the sentence starts with Not only, the first half inverts.
list.wrong: Not only he sang, but he also danced.
list.right: Not only did he sing, but he also danced.
list.trap: The inversion after a sentence-initial Not only is the whole point of the question.

list.name: No sooner ... than / Hardly ... when
list.rule: No sooner pairs with than. Hardly and Scarcely pair with when. Both invert the verb and take the past perfect first.
list.wrong: No sooner he arrived when the rain started.
list.right: No sooner had he arrived than the rain started.
list.trap: Pairing no sooner with when, or hardly with than, loses the grammar mark on its own.

list.name: The moment / As soon as
list.rule: Two things happen one right after the other, and neither half inverts.
list.wrong: The moment did he arrive, the rain started.
list.right: The moment he arrived, the rain started.
list.trap: This one does NOT invert, unlike no sooner. The two look similar and are treated the same by mistake.

list.name: In order to / So as to
list.cue: in order to, so as to, so that
list.rule: In order to and so as to take a plain verb. So that takes a full clause.
list.wrong: He woke early so that to catch the bus.
list.right: He woke early in order to catch the bus. / He woke early so that he could catch the bus.
list.trap: So that needs a subject and a modal: so that he could, so that they would.

list.name: Cleft sentence with It was
list.cue: It was ... who / It was ... that
list.rule: Put the emphasised part after It was, and everything else after who or that.
list.wrong: It was Aaron who he broke the window.
list.right: It was Aaron who broke the window.
list.trap: The old subject is not repeated after who. This is the same error as in relative clauses.

list.name: Prefer ... to
list.rule: Prefer takes to: prefer swimming to running. Would rather takes a plain verb and than: would rather swim than run.
list.wrong: He prefers swimming than running.
list.right: He prefers swimming to running.
list.trap: Than belongs to would rather, and to belongs to prefer. Swapping them is the standard error.

list.name: It is / has been ... since
list.rule: It has been plus the length of time plus since plus past simple.
list.wrong: It has been three years since he has moved here.
list.right: It has been three years since he moved here.
list.trap: The verb after since goes into the simple past, not the present perfect.

list.name: Used to
list.rule: Used to describes a past habit that has stopped, and is followed by a plain verb.
list.wrong: He used to played football every Sunday.
list.right: He used to play football every Sunday.
list.trap: The past is already carried by used, so the second verb stays plain.

list.name: Neither / Nor and So
list.cue: so did, neither did, nor did
list.rule: Agreement with a positive statement uses So plus auxiliary plus subject. Agreement with a negative uses Neither or Nor plus auxiliary plus subject.
list.wrong: She did not go, and neither I did.
list.right: She did not go, and neither did I.
list.trap: The auxiliary comes before the subject in both forms. This is an inversion.

list.name: The more ... the more
list.cue: The more, The harder, The longer
list.rule: Two comparatives, each starting its own half, with a comma between.
list.wrong: The more he practised, he improved more.
list.right: The more he practised, the more he improved.
list.trap: Both halves need the plus a comparative. Only doing it once is the usual slip.

list.name: Regret / apologise for + -ing
list.rule: These verbs take an -ing form, not a to form.
list.wrong: He apologised to break the window.
list.right: He apologised for breaking the window.
list.trap: The preposition for is compulsory with apologise, and it forces the -ing.

list.name: Suggest / insist / recommend that
list.cue: suggested that, insisted that, recommended that
list.rule: These take that plus subject plus a plain verb, with no to and no -s.
list.wrong: The teacher suggested him to rewrite the essay.
list.right: The teacher suggested that he rewrite the essay.
list.trap: Suggest never takes a person followed by to. Advise and tell do, which is what causes the mix-up.

spelling.note: Roughly half the Editing marks are spelling. These are the words that appear in PSLE editing passages year after year, and the four rules that cover most of the rest.

rules.rule: i before e except after c, when the sound is ee
rules.examples: believe, achieve, relief, but receive, ceiling, deceive
rules.exceptions: Not for other sounds: their, weird, foreign, neighbour, height.

rules.rule: Double the last letter when adding -ing or -ed to a short stressed syllable
rules.examples: stop becomes stopping, begin becomes beginning, prefer becomes preferred
rules.exceptions: Do not double when the stress is on the first syllable: visit becomes visiting, offer becomes offered.

rules.rule: Change y to i before a suffix, unless a vowel comes before the y
rules.examples: happy becomes happiness, carry becomes carried, city becomes cities
rules.exceptions: play becomes played, enjoy becomes enjoyable, because a vowel comes before the y.

rules.rule: Drop the silent e before a suffix that starts with a vowel
rules.examples: hope becomes hoping, use becomes usable, come becomes coming
rules.exceptions: Keep it before a consonant suffix: hopeful, useless, careful.

rules.rule: -ful as a suffix has one l
rules.exceptions: The word full on its own keeps both.

vocabRescue.note: This is what you do when knowledge runs out. You will meet words in Paper 2 that you have never seen, particularly in the non-narrative passage and the campaign poster, because those texts are written for adults and then set for twelve-year-olds. Not knowing the word is normal. Having no method is what costs the mark.

ladder.title: The six steps, in this order
ladder.intro: Work down the list and stop as soon as one option survives alone. Most items are decided by step three.

steps.do: Decide what KIND of word the gap needs.
steps.how: Look at the word immediately before and immediately after. After a or the, a naming word is coming. After was, were or seemed, a describing word usually is. After to, a plain verb.
steps.kills: Usually one or two options, in five seconds, without understanding any of them.

steps.do: Decide whether the missing word is POSITIVE or NEGATIVE.
steps.how: Find the signal words around it: fortunately, unfortunately, however, although, despite, sadly, thankfully, instead, yet, but. They tell you the direction even when the words are unknown.
steps.kills: Every option pointing the wrong way, whatever it means.

steps.do: Break the word into its PARTS.
steps.how: A prefix at the front changes the direction, a root in the middle carries the meaning, a suffix at the end sets the word class. Unmistakable: un- means not, mistake is the root, so it means cannot be got wrong.
steps.kills: The options whose parts point somewhere else entirely.

steps.do: Test the COMPANY the word keeps.
steps.how: Read the gap together with the word next to it and ask whether you have ever heard that pair. Heavy rain, not strong rain. Make a decision, not do a decision. Commit an offence, not make an offence.
steps.kills: The option that means the right thing but does not go there.

steps.do: Match the STRENGTH to the event.
steps.how: If several options survive, they are usually a ladder of the same idea. Ask how big the event is: annoyed, cross, furious, livid are not interchangeable.
steps.kills: The option that is right in kind but wrong in size.

steps.do: Read the whole sentence back with your answer in it.
steps.how: In your head, at normal speed, from the capital letter to the full stop.
steps.kills: The answer that was chosen from the gap alone and falls apart across the whole sentence.

clueTypes.title: Where the meaning is hiding
clueTypes.intro: The passage almost always defines a hard word somewhere near it. There are only six places it hides.

list.signals: is, means, that is, in other words, or, known as, commas or dashes around a phrase
list.example: The reservoir was becoming eutrophic, that is, so rich in nutrients that algae smothered everything else.
list.howToUse: The passage has already told you. Read the words immediately after the comma or the dash.

list.signals: but, however, unlike, whereas, although, instead, on the other hand
list.example: Her brother was gregarious; she, however, preferred to eat alone.
list.howToUse: The unknown word means roughly the OPPOSITE of the part you do understand.

list.signals: such as, for instance, including, like, e.g.
list.example: Nocturnal creatures, such as owls and bats, hunt after dark.
list.howToUse: Work backwards from the examples. What do owls and bats have in common? They are active at night.

list.signals: because, so, therefore, as a result, consequently, which led to
list.example: The soil was arid, so nothing the farmers planted survived.
list.howToUse: The result tells you the cause. Nothing survived, so arid must mean very dry.

list.signals: commas in a series, and, as well as, along with
list.example: He packed a torch, a compass, a whistle and a tarpaulin.
list.howToUse: A word takes its meaning from the company it is listed with. All of these are outdoor survival items.

list.signals: the writer's opinion words nearby, exclamation marks, praise or criticism
list.example: The council's decision was described as prudent, and residents thanked them warmly.
list.howToUse: If the surrounding words praise, the unknown word is positive. Residents thanked them, so prudent must be a good thing.

morphology.title: Break the word into parts
morphology.intro: About seventy per cent of hard English words are built from parts that repeat. You do not need to have seen the whole word before if you recognise its pieces.

suffixes.example: action, decision, movement, kindness, ability, appearance, silence

suffixes.means: makes an adverb, how something is done

confusables.title: The pairs that are set on purpose
confusables.intro: In an MCQ, two options that differ by a letter or two are never an accident. That pair is the question.

collocations.title: Words that must travel together
collocations.intro: A collocation is a pair English has simply fixed. There is no rule to work it out from, which is why they are tested, and why they are learned in pairs.

domains.title: The specific words the exam actually uses

whenStuck.title: The last thirty seconds
whenStuck.intro: When the method has run out and the clock has not, these are the rules that give you the best remaining chance.

rules.rule: Never leave it blank. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so a blank throws away a one-in-four chance for nothing.
Eliminate first, then choose. Two options you can rule out turn a guess from one-in-four into one-in-two.
If two options mean nearly the same thing, neither is usually the answer. The correct option is normally the one that is different from the rest in some way.
Do not reject an option because you have never seen the word. Unfamiliar is not the same as wrong, and the hard word is often correct precisely because the easy ones fail on collocation.
Write the ordinary word that definitely fits rather than the impressive word that might. A simple correct word earns the mark; a sophisticated near-miss earns nothing.
If nothing comes, write the smallest sensible word: a preposition, an article, an auxiliary. Function words are the most common answers and the cheapest guesses.
If you cannot find the error on a line, check the verb first, then the plural, then the spelling of the longest word. Those three cover most items.
Write something for every question. A partly right answer often scores; an empty line never does.
If you do not know the answer, answer the question word anyway using the passage's own subject matter. Markers award points, not perfection.
If you cannot get the whole sentence, still write one. The grammar mark and the meaning mark are separate, so half a success is still a mark.
